# `missing-deinit-poison`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: style · Profile: strict · Default: off · Fixes: quick fix · Options: none

Reports a `deinit` method that releases resources through a mutable receiver
pointer but does not end with `self.* = undefined;`.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

After `deinit` releases what a value owns, its fields still hold the freed
slices, closed handles and stale lengths. A later `deinit`, or any other use
of the value, then reads them as if they were live: a double free, a write to
a closed file, or a read from memory another allocation now owns. Ending
`deinit` with `self.* = undefined;`, as the standard library does, marks the
whole value undefined, so safe builds fill it with `0xaa` and the first later
use fails close to the mistake instead of corrupting something else.

## When it fires

It reports a method named `deinit` whose first parameter is a mutable pointer
(`self: *T`) when its body calls a release method (`free`, `destroy`,
`deinit`, `close`, `join`, `detach` or `unlock`) and its last statement is
not `self.* = undefined;`. A receiver taken by value or as `*const T` is not
reported, nor an empty body, a body that discards the receiver with
`_ = self;`, a body with a `return` (the poison would not run on that path),
a body that assigns `self.*` to reset the value or ends by assigning one of
its fields (`self.fd = -1;` marks the released state on purpose), and a body
that frees the receiver itself, as in `allocator.destroy(self)`. The quick fix appends
`self.* = undefined;`; the same edit is offered on any such `deinit` as the
"Poison after deinit" action.

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
const std = @import("std");

const Buffer = struct {
    bytes: []u8,

    fn deinit(self: *Buffer, gpa: std.mem.Allocator) void {
        gpa.free(self.bytes);
    }
};
```
